title: The Worst Dinner in the Universe

pages.text:
Saturday seventy-one, 5:30. The pizza boxes lay open on the living room floor, the air thick with the smell of pepperoni and cardboard. We sat in a circle of paper plates.

Dad was standing, which he only did when he was nervous. His hands flapped a little, like a bird trying to remember how to fly.

"To this house," he said. His voice cracked on the word *house*. He swallowed. "It has been... a lot. A lot of boxes. A lot of moving. But I think it is the best house we have ever had, because it is the one we are leaving behind."

He looked at Mom. She was crying, not the silent kind, but the loud, snotty kind. I had heard this toast seventy times. I had the words in my head. I knew the pause before "cactus adventures." I knew the way he would wipe his eye with his thumb. I wanted to scream. I wanted to hit the wall. I wanted the floor to swallow me whole.

"To the future," Dad said, raising his slice. "Which is mostly cactus, but full of adventure."

"Stop," I said. "Please just stop talking."
pages.image: A big man with a mustache stands on tiptoes holding a pizza slice, looking hopeful; a woman with curly hair in a clip sits on a floor cushion wiping tears; an 11-year-old boy in a red hoodie sits rigidly, looking angry.

pages.text:
My voice came out louder than I intended, bouncing off the bare walls until the room felt too small for all of us.

Dad froze. His slice hung there, a long strand of cheese stretching from the tip like the elastic on a gym sock that is about to snap.

"What do you mean, stop?" he asked.

"I mean stop," I said. "Stop pretending. You can't fix it with words. You can't fix it with puns. Those things you say are pathetic. They do not make the moving truck go away."

Mom’s hands slammed down on the edge of the pizza box. She stared at me with wide eyes, her pencil still tucked behind her ear, and the house went so quiet I could hear the refrigerator humming.

"Max," she said, and her voice was the kind of quiet that makes your knees feel like wet paper.

"I am not done," I said. "Your lists don't work. I have checked. You have checked every single box, and we are still sad. You cannot put a checkmark next to 'not being scared.'"

I stood up, and my knees knocked into the table hard enough to rattle the plates. I didn't care. For one second I was taller than all of them. I was the one in charge. I was the one with the power, because I was the one who was right.
pages.image: Max stands up abruptly, pointing a finger at his father, who holds a pizza slice with a long strand of cheese; his mother sits with hands flat on a pizza box, looking stunned and worried.

pages.text:
I turned to Tessa. She sat cross-legged, a drumstick in her right hand, tapping it against her knee. *Tap, tap, tap.* The rhythm was steady, a machine gun of wood and impatience.

"And you," I said, pointing a finger at her. I aimed specifically at the purple streak in her hair. "You think you are the only one who is scared. You think you are the only one who is going to fail."

Tessa stopped tapping. The stick hovered in the air, frozen mid-beat.

"You are going to get to that new school," I continued, my voice climbing. "And nobody is going to talk to you. They are going to wear headphones and look at their phones, ignoring everything around them. And you are going to sit in the bathroom and cry because you don't know how to be cool again. You know it is going to happen, don't you?"

The drumstick dropped. It hit the floor with a sharp *thwack* that sounded louder than it had any right to be.

Tessa stared at me, her face draining of color. She didn't say anything. She just looked at me, and the silence between us felt thin and stretched, like the plastic wrap on a container of leftovers. I had seen that fear in her eyes every time she looked at the moving boxes. I had seen it clearly. And now I had thrown it back at her like a rock.
pages.image: A teenage girl with a purple streak in her hair and headphones around her neck sits on a floor cushion, staring shock at a boy; a wooden drumstick lies on the carpet near her hand; pizza boxes surround them.

pages.text:
Then I looked at Gus. He sat in his green T. rex costume, holding a slice of pizza that was mostly crust. His eyes were big behind the dinosaur hood, watching me.

"And it is a costume, Gus," I said, my voice shaking though I didn't care. "It is just fabric. It doesn't protect anybody. It doesn't make you a dinosaur. You are just a kid in a suit who is going to have to sleep in a weird bed in a weird state."

Gus’s lip trembled. It was a small, thin line inside the hood. He didn't roar. He didn't say a word. He just looked at me with a face I didn't recognize. It was a face of betrayal.

Waffles whined. It was a low, sad sound. The dog put his head down between his paws.

Mom was standing up. Her hand was on her mouth. She looked like she was going to be sick.

I looked at all of them. I looked at the pizza. I looked at the bare walls. I was the worst person in the world. I knew it. I knew it in my bones.

I ran.
pages.image: A small child in a green T. rex costume sits on the floor, looking sad and trembling; a chubby corgi with a white paw lies down with its head between its paws; an 11-year-old boy runs toward a door in the background.

pages.text:
I skipped my room and headed straight for the garage. I climbed the ladder to the roof, where the air felt cool against my sweaty hoodie and the stars were scattered across the dark sky like dropped sugar. I sat on the shingles and buried my face in my hands, waiting for the clock to strike and the world to reset. I wanted to wake up with them having forgotten. I wanted to be the good brother, the funny one, the one who actually laughed at Dad's terrible jokes.

Footsteps crunched on the porch gravel.

"Max?"

It was Mom. She stood at the garage door, looking up at me. She wasn't yelling, and she wasn't angry. She just looked exhausted, her pencil still tucked behind her ear.

"I don't know what happened tonight," she said, her voice soft and quiet. "But I love you."

I wanted to tell her I loved her back. I wanted to apologize for being terrible. I wanted to fix everything. But before I could get a word out, a loud, angry roar came from inside the house.

"RAAAAWR."

I blinked, my head still resting on my knees. The stars had vanished, replaced by a grey morning light.

I was lying in my bed. Gus was sitting on my chest.

"RAAAAWR," he said.

I looked at the clock on the wall. It read 6:47.

I realized then that you can't say sorry to someone who never heard you be awful. I found that out exactly seven seconds after the worst night of my life.
pages.image: Max lies in bed, eyes wide open, looking shocked; Gus in a green T. rex costume sits on his chest roaring; morning light streams through a window; a cuckoo clock is visible on the wall.
